The story contains a surreal and surprising turn when it is revealed that the woman the narrator is following shares the exact physical characteristics and injuries of the burned, upholstered chair left on the curb (wearing a green blouse with yellow flowers, and having a blackened, burned left arm). 

Despite how bizarre and unexpected this revelation is, it feels entirely appropriate within the context of the narrative. From the opening lines, the story establishes an eerie, slightly absurd atmosphere where people put furniture out for a flood "as though a flood were an inspection," and the narrator leaves his home to buy batteries he doesn't need. Furthermore, the narrator's background as an inventory clerk who obsessively catalogues the "presence and condition" of household objects makes him the perfect lens through which to blur the line between a piece of damaged furniture and a human being. Early clues—such as the woman's initial warning ("Don't sit there")—take on a haunting, fitting resonance in hindsight.
